match.reason: The closest bank point, Antiderivatives, teaches the power rule and the constant of integration algebraically, but it does not teach that the graphs of antiderivatives differ only by a vertical shift, so no bank point teaches the new graphical idea.

draft.title: Graphs of antiderivatives
card: An antiderivative of f is a function F whose derivative is f. So F′(x) = f(x).
Any two antiderivatives of f differ by a constant. Their graphs are vertical shifts of each other, with the same shape.
Where f is positive, F is increasing. Where f is negative, F is decreasing. Where f = 0, F has a stationary point.
Example: if f is a straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 2 from below to above, F has a minimum at x = 2.
draft.remember: The sign of f gives the slope of F, and F can be shifted up or down.

a.q: The graph of f is above the x-axis for 1 < x < 4. What does the graph of an antiderivative F do on that interval?
a.why: F′ = f, and f is positive there, so F is increasing. F being above the x-axis depends on the shift, so it is not guaranteed.
a.clue: F′ = f, so the sign of f gives the slope of F.

b.q: f crosses the x-axis at x = 3 from above to below. What does an antiderivative F have at x = 3?
b.why: F′ = f is positive before x = 3 and negative after, so F rises then falls. This gives a local maximum. A minimum would need f to go from negative to positive.
b.clue: Check whether F rises or falls on each side of x = 3.

final.title: Graphs of antiderivatives
card: An antiderivative of \(f\) is a function \(F\) whose derivative is \(f\). So \(F'(x) = f(x)\).
Any two antiderivatives of \(f\) differ by a constant. Their graphs are vertical shifts of each other, with the same shape.
Where \(f\) is positive, \(F\) is increasing. Where \(f\) is negative, \(F\) is decreasing. Where \(f = 0\), \(F\) has a stationary point.
Example: if \(f\) is a straight line crossing the x-axis at \(x = 2\) from below to above, \(F\) has a minimum at \(x = 2\).

4.alt: The dashed line \(y = f(x) = x - 2\) crosses the x-axis at \(x = 2\), from below to above. The solid curve \(y = F(x)\), an antiderivative of \(f\), decreases while \(f\) is negative and increases while \(f\) is positive, so it has a minimum at \((2, -1)\).

final.remember: The sign of \(f\) gives the gradient of \(F\), and \(F\) can be shifted up or down.

a.q: The graph of \(f\) is above the x-axis for \(1 < x < 4\). What does the graph of an antiderivative \(F\) do on that interval?
a.why: \(F' = f\), and \(f\) is positive there, so \(F\) is increasing. \(F\) being above the x-axis depends on the shift, so it is not guaranteed.
a.clue: \(F' = f\), so the sign of \(f\) gives the gradient of \(F\).

b.q: \(f\) crosses the x-axis at \(x = 3\) from above to below. What does an antiderivative \(F\) have at \(x = 3\)?
b.why: \(F' = f\) is positive before \(x = 3\) and negative after, so \(F\) rises then falls. This gives a local maximum. A minimum would need \(f\) to go from negative to positive.
b.clue: Check whether \(F\) rises or falls on each side of \(x = 3\).
